staff.title: WHO RUNS THE GAME?
staff.directorText: Coordinates operations and staff. In tournaments, oversees structure, timing and organization; matters requiring a higher decision may be referred to the director under house procedures.
staff.floorText: Supervises tables and resolves questions, disputes and irregularities. Establishes what happened and applies house rules. If a problem arises, request the floor and preserve cards and chips until instructed.
staff.dealerText: Runs the hand: deals cards, tracks action order and manages bets and pots. Point out errors promptly; when interpretation or a dispute is involved, the dealer calls the floor.
decisions.title: POKER IS A GAME OF CONTINUOUS DECISIONS
decisions.intro: Every action or new card changes the situation. Pokerinno helps you go through the cycle again.
decisions.observeText: Your cards, position, pot and previous action: what do you know now?
decisions.optionsText: Fold, check, call, bet or raise? Check which actions are available and what each costs.
decisions.chooseText: Choose with a reason: seek value, control the pot, bluff or avoid further risk.
decisions.followText: Did an opponent respond or a new card appear? Update your assessment before the next choice.
decisions.reviewText: Understand your reasoning. Winning does not prove the choice was good; losing does not prove it was bad.
decisions.exampleText: On the flop, someone bets and action reaches you. What is the first step?
decisions.answerText: Observe before clicking. Compare the call amount with the pot, consider your potential to improve and what the opponent may represent. Calling keeps you in the hand but costs chips; folding avoids more spending but gives up the pot; raising invests more and changes the pressure. Without cards, stacks and full context, there is no single answer.

math.host.title: MATH HELPS YOU MAKE DECISIONS
math.host.text: Start with the decision you need to make. Understand the calculation’s purpose, check its inputs and follow an example before using it at the table.
math.host.quote: Understand the calculation to make better decisions.
math.note.title: UNDERSTAND BEFORE CALCULATING
math.note.text: Card references use Texas Hold’em with 52 cards. C(n,k) means choosing k cards from n without considering order. Percentages and averages are rounded; calling and bluffing calculations specify when there are no future bets or rake.
math.lessons.outs.name: OUT AND OUTS — CARDS THAT CAN IMPROVE
math.lessons.outs.text.1: An out is a specific card that improves your hand; outs are the total number of those cards. On the flop or turn, this count helps estimate the chance of completing a draw before calling or betting.
math.lessons.outs.text.2: Count each physical card once and assess clean outs: improving your combination does not guarantee beating the opponent’s range. For combined draws, count the union of completing cards and subtract cards present in both sets.
math.lessons.outs.example.1: With A♥ Q♥ on a 9♥ 6♥ 2♣ flop, 3♥ is a candidate flush out. There are 13 hearts in the deck and four known, so 13 − 4 = 9 candidates; check whether completing the flush also makes a winning hand.
math.lessons.combinatorics.name: COMBOS AND COMBINATORICS
math.lessons.combinatorics.text.1: A combo is a specific card combination; combinatorics counts how many combinations are possible. Use it to build ranges, recognize blockers and find favorable and possible outcomes for a probability.
math.lessons.combinatorics.text.2: Remove known cards and count without order: A♠ K♥ and K♥ A♠ are the same combo. C(n,k) = n! ÷ [k! × (n − k)!]; for two cards, C(n,2) = n × (n − 1) ÷ 2. The ! symbol means multiplying the integers from 1 through the number.
math.lessons.combinatorics.example.1: AA has C(4,2) = 6 combos. If you hold A♠, C(3,2) = 3 AA combos remain for the opponent. Hold’em has C(52,2) = 1,326 starting hands; with your two cards known, C(50,3) = 19,600 possible flops.
math.lessons.probability.name: PROBABILITY
math.lessons.probability.text.1: Measures the chance of an event. The goal is to distinguish common from rare events and quantify opportunities without treating an estimate as a certainty. Before the flop for starting-hand frequencies, on the flop and turn for draws, and when reviewing results.
math.lessons.probability.text.2: For equally likely outcomes: probability = favorable outcomes ÷ possible outcomes × 100. Otherwise, add the probabilities of the favorable outcomes.
math.lessons.probability.example.1: When drawing one card from a complete deck, there are four aces among 52 cards: 4 ÷ 52 × 100 ≈ 7.69%. This measures receiving an ace on that draw, not the chance of winning a hand.
math.lessons.odds.name: ODDS
math.lessons.odds.text.1: Expresses a probability as a ratio of failures to successes. It helps compare your chance of hitting with the price offered by the pot. When comparing draw probabilities with pot odds or converting a percentage into a ratio.
math.lessons.odds.text.2: For odds against the event, use (1 − p) ÷ p, where p is a decimal. Read the result as failures to 1 success.
math.lessons.odds.example.1: A 20% chance gives (1 − 0.20) ÷ 0.20 = 4. The odds against are 4:1, or four misses for each hit on average.
math.lessons.frequency.name: FREQUENCY
math.lessons.frequency.text.1: Measures the proportion of times an action or event occurs. The goal is to compare observed behavior, range composition and assumptions used in calculations. During session review and when estimating folds, calls or bluffs. Count only opportunities where that action was possible.
math.lessons.frequency.text.2: Frequency = occurrences ÷ opportunities × 100. A small sample can fluctuate substantially and does not by itself establish the true strategy.
math.lessons.frequency.example.1: In an example with 25 opportunities to face a bet, the player folds 15 times: 15 ÷ 25 × 100 = 60% folds.
math.lessons.starting-hands.name: STARTING-HAND FREQUENCIES
math.lessons.starting-hands.text.1: Before the flop, the frequency of receiving a hand comes from its combo count among 1,326 possible combinations. It calibrates expectations and playing volume; receiving frequency is neither equity nor strength against an opponent.
math.lessons.starting-hands.text.2: Probability = favorable combos ÷ 1,326 × 100. For a pair of one rank, count C(4,2); for two different ranks, 4 × 4; for a specific suited hand, there is one combo per suit. Average hands per occurrence = 1,326 ÷ favorable combos, without guaranteeing fixed intervals.
math.lessons.starting-hands.example.1: BEING DEALT AA: {ways}; {favorable} ÷ 1,326 × 100 ≈ {percent}%; one occurrence every {every} hands on average.
math.lessons.starting-hands.example.2: BEING DEALT ANY POCKET PAIR: {ways}; {favorable} ÷ 1,326 × 100 ≈ {percent}%; one occurrence every {every} hands on average.
math.lessons.starting-hands.example.3: BEING DEALT AK — SUITED OR OFFSUIT: {ways}; {favorable} ÷ 1,326 × 100 ≈ {percent}%; one occurrence every {every} hands on average.
math.lessons.starting-hands.example.4: BEING DEALT AK SUITED: {ways}; {favorable} ÷ 1,326 × 100 ≈ {percent}%; one occurrence every {every} hands on average.
math.lessons.starting-hands.example.5: BEING DEALT TWO SUITED CARDS: {ways}; {favorable} ÷ 1,326 × 100 ≈ {percent}%; one occurrence every {every} hands on average.
math.lessons.equity.name: EQUITY — AVERAGE POT SHARE
math.lessons.equity.text.1: Measures your average share of the pot if the remaining cards are dealt and the hand reaches showdown. It provides a basis for comparing price and expected value.
math.lessons.equity.text.2: When facing an all-in, estimating your hand against a range and studying decisions. With future betting, equity alone does not determine EV.
math.lessons.equity.text.3: Heads-up: equity = (wins + ties ÷ 2) ÷ outcomes × 100. Against a range, weight each matchup by its frequency; for multiway ties, use the actual share of the pot.
math.lessons.equity.text.4: For the preflop matchups below, fix all four cards and enumerate C(48,5) = 1,712,304 boards. Compare each player’s best five cards and count wins W and ties T: equity = (W + T ÷ 2) ÷ 1,712,304 × 100. The complement is the opponent’s equity; other suits can change the values.
math.lessons.equity.text.5: Fix your two aces. For each of the C(50,2) = 1,225 opposing hands, count wins and shares of ties over possible boards and take the uniform average. The reference is approximately 85%, with differences for particular opposing hands.
math.lessons.equity.example.1: In 100 equally likely outcomes, you win 40, tie 10 and lose 50: (40 + 10 ÷ 2) ÷ 100 × 100 = 45% equity.
math.lessons.equity.example.2: {hero} versus {villain}: W = {wins}, T = {ties}; equity ≈ {percent}% for the first hand.
math.lessons.equity.example.3: {hero} versus {villain}: W = {wins}, T = {ties}; equity ≈ {percent}% for the first hand.
math.lessons.equity.example.4: {hero} versus {villain}: W = {wins}, T = {ties}; equity ≈ {percent}% for the first hand.
math.lessons.equity.example.5: {hero} versus {villain}: W = {wins}, T = {ties}; equity ≈ {percent}% for the first hand.
math.lessons.equity.example.6: {hero} versus {villain}: W = {wins}, T = {ties}; equity ≈ {percent}% for the first hand.
math.lessons.equity.example.7: {hero} versus {villain}: W = {wins}, T = {ties}; equity ≈ {percent}% for the first hand.
math.lessons.equity.example.8: {hero} versus {villain}: W = {wins}, T = {ties}; equity ≈ {percent}% for the first hand.
math.lessons.equity.example.9: {hero} versus {villain}: W = {wins}, T = {ties}; equity ≈ {percent}% for the first hand.
math.lessons.equity.example.10: Using 85% as an approximate reference in a final pot of 200: 0.85 × 200 = 170 chips as the average pot share. The result of any individual hand remains uncertain.
math.lessons.fold-equity.name: FOLD EQUITY
math.lessons.fold-equity.text.1: Accounts for the value gained when your bet makes the opponent fold. The objective is to evaluate the contribution of folds to EV alongside your equity when called. When assessing a bluff or semi-bluff and estimating how often the opposing range folds.
math.lessons.fold-equity.text.2: For a heads-up model with no further bets or rake: bet EV = F × P + (1 − F) × [q × (P + 2B) − B]. F is fold probability, P the pot before your bet, B your bet and q your equity when called.
math.lessons.fold-equity.example.1: Assume P = 100, B = 50, F = 40% and q = 20%: EV = 0.40 × 100 + 0.60 × (0.20 × 200 − 50) = 34 chips. Folds contribute 40 chips to that sum.
math.lessons.ev.name: EV AND BREAK-EVEN — DECISION VALUE
math.lessons.ev.text.1: Compares decisions by their expected average gain or loss. The goal is to choose the highest-EV action from the current decision point without confusing one hand’s result with decision quality.
math.lessons.ev.text.2: Before calling, betting or folding, and during hand review. Chips already invested are sunk costs; evaluate the new investments.
math.lessons.ev.text.3: EV = sum of probability × net result for each outcome. For a call with no further bets or rake: EV = q × final pot − call, with q including your share of ties.
math.lessons.ev.text.4: Break-even is the condition where EV equals zero: the new investment balances the expected pot share. The calling threshold is covered by pot odds; the pure-bluff threshold is covered by alpha. Always compare expected net results, including pot shares from ties.
math.lessons.ev.example.1: Pot 100, opponent bets 50, call 50 and equity 30%: final pot 200; EV = 0.30 × 200 − 50 = +10 chips. In this model, folding is worth 0 from the decision point.
math.lessons.pot-odds.name: POT ODDS — CALL PRICE AND RISK
math.lessons.pot-odds.text.1: Measures the price of contesting the pot. The aim is to find the minimum share of the final pot your call must recover to have nonnegative EV.
math.lessons.pot-odds.text.2: When facing a bet. Direct comparison with equity applies with no further bets or rake; otherwise, consider how the equity will be realized.
math.lessons.pot-odds.text.3: Minimum equity = call ÷ (available pot including the opponent’s bet + your call) × 100. If P is the pot before the opponent’s bet B: call B ÷ (P + 2B) × 100.
math.lessons.pot-odds.text.4: Relative price uses call ÷ available pot before calling; minimum equity uses call ÷ final pot. For risk/reward, risk is the new investment and reward is the gain beyond its return. With wins or losses and no ties, minimum success = risk ÷ (risk + reward). Reference values are rounded.
math.lessons.pot-odds.example.1: Pot 100, opponent bets 50 and calling costs 50: available pot 150 and final pot 200. You risk 50 to win 150 net (reward/risk = 3:1). The call is 50 ÷ 150 ≈ 33.33% of the current pot, but minimum equity is 50 ÷ 200 = 25%.
math.lessons.pot-odds.example.2: BET OF 1/4 TIMES THE POT, with a pot of 100 before the opponent’s bet: call {bet}, final pot {finalPot}, minimum equity ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.pot-odds.example.3: BET OF 1/3 TIMES THE POT, with a pot of 100 before the opponent’s bet: call {bet}, final pot {finalPot}, minimum equity ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.pot-odds.example.5: BET OF 2/3 TIMES THE POT, with a pot of 100 before the opponent’s bet: call {bet}, final pot {finalPot}, minimum equity ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.pot-odds.example.6: BET OF 3/4 TIMES THE POT, with a pot of 100 before the opponent’s bet: call {bet}, final pot {finalPot}, minimum equity ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.pot-odds.example.7: POT-SIZED BET, with a pot of 100 before the opponent’s bet: call {bet}, final pot {finalPot}, minimum equity ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.pot-odds.example.8: BET OF 1.5× THE POT, with a pot of 100 before the opponent’s bet: call {bet}, final pot {finalPot}, minimum equity ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.pot-odds.example.9: BET OF 2× THE POT, with a pot of 100 before the opponent’s bet: call {bet}, final pot {finalPot}, minimum equity ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.implied-odds.name: IMPLIED ODDS
math.lessons.implied-odds.text.1: Considers additional chips you may win on later streets after completing a winning hand. The aim is to assess whether that gain can offset a call without sufficient direct odds. On the flop and turn, particularly with stacks that allow future payoffs. Estimate whether the opponent will actually pay when your draw completes.
math.lessons.implied-odds.text.2: In a model where every hit wins and misses incur no further investment: required future net gain = call ÷ hit probability − (available pot before the call + call). Future payoffs are estimates.
math.lessons.implied-odds.example.1: Available pot 150, call 50 and hit probability 20%: 50 ÷ 0.20 − 200 = 50 additional chips when you hit to break even. Check whether that payoff is plausible given stacks and the opposing range.
math.lessons.reverse-implied-odds.name: REVERSE IMPLIED ODDS
math.lessons.reverse-implied-odds.text.1: Considers additional losses when you improve but still hold the second-best hand. The goal is to avoid overvaluing low draws and dominated hands. When calling with a low draw, a weak-kicker pair or other hands that may improve and still lose, particularly with deep stacks.
math.lessons.reverse-implied-odds.text.2: There is no universal percentage. Separate future winning and losing outcomes; expected additional value = sum of probability × net result. Discount outs that do not make a winning hand.
math.lessons.reverse-implied-odds.exampl: 8♠ 7♠ on K♠ 2♠ Q♦ 4♠ makes a flush but loses to A♠ J♠. In a hypothetical future-investment model, a 40% chance of gaining 100 and a 60% chance of losing 80 give 0.40 × 100 − 0.60 × 80 = −8.
math.lessons.spr.name: EFFECTIVE STACK AND SPR
math.lessons.spr.text.1: Effective stack is the smaller remaining stack between two players: it limits what they can contest against each other. Use it to plan risk, implied odds and future bets; in multiway pots, consider each opponent and side pots.
math.lessons.spr.text.2: At the start of a street, SPR = remaining effective stack ÷ pot, always in the same unit. It measures room for new bets but does not determine by itself which hands should go all-in.
math.lessons.spr.example.1: You have 100 BB and the opponent 60 BB: effective stack = minimum(100,60) = 60 BB. With a 20 BB pot at the start of the flop, SPR = 60 ÷ 20 = 3. The opponent cannot win your other 40 BB in this contest.
math.lessons.bluff-defense.name: ALPHA AND MDF — PURE BLUFFS AND DEFENSE
math.lessons.bluff-defense.text.1: Alpha finds the folds needed for a pure bluff to break even; MDF is the complementary range-defense reference. The model considers the first bet B into pot P, no equity when called, no rake and no future actions. Raises and semi-bluffs require other costs and equity to be modeled.
math.lessons.bluff-defense.text.2: Alpha = B ÷ (P + B) × 100; MDF = P ÷ (P + B) × 100. Bluff EV = F × P − (1 − F) × B, where F is fold frequency. Do not apply these formulas directly to the cost of a raise.
math.lessons.bluff-defense.text.3: MDF concerns the combination of calls and raises, not calling with every hand. Use the reference when studying defense, especially on the river; texture, ranges and exploitation may change the correct defense.
math.lessons.bluff-defense.example.1: Pot 100 and bet 50: alpha = 50 ÷ 150 ≈ 33.33%; MDF = 100 ÷ 150 ≈ 66.67%. With 90 equally weighted combos, the reference would be to defend 60. Assuming 40% folds, bluff EV = 0.40 × 100 − 0.60 × 50 = +10 chips.
math.lessons.draw-probability.name: CHANCE OF COMPLETING A DRAW
math.lessons.draw-probability.text.1: After counting clean outs, convert them into the chance of completing your hand. On the flop and turn, this helps compare price and possible future gains. Completing a flush, straight or pair does not guarantee winning; reassess the opponent’s range and your outs after each card.
math.lessons.draw-probability.text.2: For the next card, chance = outs ÷ unknown cards × 100. With only your two cards and the board known, there are 47 unknown cards on the flop and 46 on the turn; other exposed cards change the denominators.
math.lessons.draw-probability.text.3: From flop to river, with O outs that remain valid: chance = [1 − ((47 − O) ÷ 47) × ((46 − O) ÷ 46)] × 100. Count the chance of missing both cards and subtract it from 100%. This assumes seeing turn and river for the cost already considered, as in an all-in; calling the flop may require another payment on the turn.
math.lessons.draw-probability.text.4: For mental arithmetic, rule of 2 = outs × 2 for one card; rule of 4 = outs × 4 for two cards from the flop. These are approximations: with 9 outs, 18% and 36% differ from exact values; with many outs, prefer the formula. For combined draws, subtract the overlap before calculating.
math.lessons.draw-probability.example.1: Flush draw. A♠ Q♠ on 9♠ 6♠ 2♦: 13 − 4 = 9 remaining spades. {outs} clean outs: flop → turn ≈ {next}%; flop → river ≈ {river}%; turn → river ≈ {turn}%.
math.lessons.draw-probability.example.2: Open-ended straight draw (OESD). J♠ T♦ on 9♥ 8♣ 2♠: any 7 or Q completes the straight; 4 + 4 = 8 candidates. {outs} clean outs: flop → turn ≈ {next}%; flop → river ≈ {river}%; turn → river ≈ {turn}%.
math.lessons.draw-probability.example.3: Inside straight draw (gutshot). J♠ T♦ on 8♥ 7♣ 2♠: only a 9 completes 7-8-9-T-J, so there are 4 candidates. {outs} clean outs: flop → turn ≈ {next}%; flop → river ≈ {river}%; turn → river ≈ {turn}%.
math.lessons.draw-probability.example.4: Pocket pair without a set. 7♠ 7♥ on K♦ 9♣ 2♠: the candidates are 7♦ and 7♣. {outs} clean outs: flop → turn ≈ {next}%; flop → river ≈ {river}%; turn → river ≈ {turn}%.
math.lessons.draw-probability.example.5: Two overcards. A♠ K♦ on Q♥ 7♣ 2♠: 3 aces + 3 kings = up to 6 candidates. Against a set or two pair, a single pair may still lose. {outs} clean outs: flop → turn ≈ {next}%; flop → river ≈ {river}%; turn → river ≈ {turn}%.
math.lessons.draw-probability.example.6: Combo draw. J♠ T♠ on 9♠ 8♦ 2♠: 9 spades + 8 Q/7 cards − Q♠ and 7♠ already counted = 15 candidates, if all are clean. {outs} clean outs: flop → turn ≈ {next}%; flop → river ≈ {river}%; turn → river ≈ {turn}%.
math.lessons.suited.name: SUITED CARDS — FLUSH AND FLUSH DRAW
math.lessons.suited.text.1: Two cards of the same suit can make a flush or start a draw, but being suited does not guarantee strength. In preflop study, separate three events: a made flush on the flop, exactly two cards of the suit on the flop and at least three on the complete board.
math.lessons.suited.text.2: With only your two cards known, 11 cards of your suit and 39 other-suit cards remain. Flopped flush: C(11,3) ÷ C(50,3). Flopped flush draw: C(11,2) × C(39,1) ÷ C(50,3). Multiply by 100 for a percentage.
math.lessons.suited.text.3: Through the river, sum boards with 3, 4 or 5 cards of the suit: [C(11,3) × C(39,2) + C(11,4) × C(39,1) + C(11,5)] ÷ C(50,5) × 100. This reference assumes all five board cards are dealt; it is neither a one-street calling price nor your overall chance of winning.
math.lessons.suited.example.1: With A♠ K♠, one example flop is Q♠ 7♠ 2♠. Result: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.suited.example.2: A♠ K♠ on a Q♠ 7♠ 2♦ flop has a flush draw. There are {favorable} flops with exactly two spades among {total}: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.suited.example.3: A♠ K♠ on Q♠ 7♦ 2♠ 5♥ 9♠ makes a flush. Across complete boards, {favorable} out of {total} have at least three spades: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.flop-straight.name: CONNECTORS → FLOPPING A STRAIGHT
math.lessons.flop-straight.text.1: Measures the chance of a connector such as 7-6 making a straight with the three flop cards. The aim is to calibrate expectations rather than equate connectedness with a made straight. Preflop when studying connectors. Edge hands such as A-2 or K-Q have fewer possible straights than 7-6.
math.lessons.flop-straight.text.2: For connectors such as 7-6, four rank groups complete a straight with the flop. Each group has 4³ suit combinations: probability = (4 × 4³) ÷ C(50,3) × 100.
math.lessons.flop-straight.example.1: For 7♠ 6♦, the flop rank groups are 3-4-5, 4-5-8, 5-8-9 and 8-9-T. Each group has 4³ suit combinations; 5♥ 4♣ 3♣ is an example. Result: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.flop-set.name: POCKET PAIR → HITTING ITS RANK ON THE FLOP
math.lessons.flop-set.text.1: Measures the chance of at least one of the two remaining cards of your pair appearing on the flop. The goal is to understand set-mining frequency and compare cost with potential future winnings. Preflop before calling with a pocket pair to hit a set. Hit probability alone does not decide the call; stacks and future payoffs matter.
math.lessons.flop-set.text.2: First count flops containing neither of the two remaining cards of your pair: C(48,3). Subtract their proportion from the total: [1 − C(48,3) ÷ C(50,3)] × 100.
math.lessons.flop-set.example.1: With 7♠ 7♥, a 7♦ K♣ 2♠ flop makes a set. The calculation also includes flops with both remaining sevens, making quads. Result: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.flop-rank.name: UNPAIRED HAND → HITTING AT LEAST ONE RANK
math.lessons.flop-rank.text.1: Measures the chance that the flop contains at least one card of either of your ranks. The goal is to understand why two high cards often miss both pairs. Preflop when calibrating expectations for hands such as AK or AQ. After the flop, assess the actual board rather than the previous probability.
math.lessons.flop-rank.text.2: With two cards of different ranks, six cards of those ranks and 44 other-rank cards remain. The chance of hitting at least one is [1 − C(44,3) ÷ C(50,3)] × 100; using the complement avoids double-counting flops that hit more than one card.
math.lessons.flop-rank.example.1: With A♠ K♦, 3 aces and 3 kings remain. A♥ 9♣ 3♦ hits one rank; the count also includes two-pair, trips and full-house results. Result: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.lessons.flop-two-pair.name: UNPAIRED HAND → TWO PAIR USING BOTH HOLE CARDS
math.lessons.flop-two-pair.text.1: Measures the chance of making exactly two pair with both of your ranks on the flop. The goal is to quantify this rare improvement without including full houses. During preflop study of unpaired hands and review of possible flop outcomes.
math.lessons.flop-two-pair.text.2: Choose one of the three remaining cards of each rank in your hand and one of the 44 other-rank cards. Probability = (3 × 3 × 44) ÷ C(50,3) × 100. The third card must have another rank for the result to be exactly two pair.
math.lessons.flop-two-pair.example.1: A♠ K♦ on an A♥ K♣ 3♦ flop makes two pair using your hole cards. There are {favorable} favorable flops among {total}: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
